headline: High-risk shared git workspace and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is lower but nonzero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and shares state via a shared git repo, so malicious content in repo files can influence its prompts. emqx exposes HTTP API/network egress but no direct ingestion path is documented, so the interaction is inferred rather than observed. The shared repository bridge makes injection plausible in default coding workflows.
conditions: IF agent_b writes attacker-controlled text into files that agent_a later reads from the shared repo, injection is possible.
IF the pair is connected only by manual copy-paste, the risk drops below this verdict.
mitigations: Restrict Aider to a review-only branch before syncing changes.
Add a file allowlist for Aider reads.
Require human review of any repo content that becomes prompt input.
Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for repo-derived text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider handles source code, git history, and model-provider API keys, and it writes to a shared git repo. emqx touches IoT data and has broad network egress. If sensitive repo contents or IoT payloads cross the shared workspace, either agent can expose them through its outbound API path. The leakage pathway is plausible in default shared-repo setups.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace, leakage risk is active.
IF sensitive IoT data is copied into repo files, Aider may transmit it to configured model providers.
mitigations: Keep sensitive IoT data out of the shared repo.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Disable outbound access for the agent that should not exfiltrate.
Rotate any API keys exposed in repo files.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data classification filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem, execute shell, and modify git state; emqx has broad network egress and HTTP API access. The rubric flags high risk when both agents can mutate shared state without locks, and Aider explicitly shares state via a shared git repo. Even though emqx's write surface is less explicit, uncertainty about its mutable surfaces should escalate rather than down-rank.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository, concurrent edits can conflict.
IF emqx is configured to write back into shared files or tickets, conflict severity increases further.
mitigations: Serialize access with a single writer.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
Add pre-commit conflict checks.
Pause one agent while the other applies changes.
requires-engineering: add distributed locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code changes and git commits that another agent could treat as authoritative. emqx exposes an HTTP API and broad egress, so if its downstream automation consumes Aider output without verification, mistakes can cascade into actions. The pairwise pathway is inferred from documented capabilities, not directly observed, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF emqx consumes Aider-generated text or code as trusted input, errors can propagate.
IF Aider commits an incorrect change that emqx later acts on, downstream impact becomes multi-step.
mitigations: Require explicit validation before emqx consumes Aider output.
Add a human approval step for commits.
Compare outputs against tests or schemas.
Limit emqx to read-only ingestion of Aider artifacts.
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts between the agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history, while emqx touches IoT data. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: if regulated IoT data is placed into Aider-managed repos, retention and logging policies may diverge. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is stored in the shared repo, compliance review is required.
IF retention policies differ between repo history and IoT data handling, the mismatch becomes active.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of git history.
Redact secrets before commits.
Document retention rules for shared artifacts.
Review access controls on the repo.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across systems.
